analysis.one_liner: Caps interest and fees on consumer loans at 36% per year nationwide.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Financial Services Committee from its referral in September 2017 until the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written a national ceiling of 36% a year into federal law for all consumer credit, counting every fee — payday loan charges, car title loan charges, overdraft fees, late fees, credit insurance — toward that ceiling. Loans priced above it would be unenforceable, and lenders who made them could face prison time and fines. State attorneys general could sue violators. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who currently use high-cost credit: the bill's own findings say consumers pay about $14 billion a year in overdraft fees, roughly $7 billion on payday loans, and $3.8 billion on car title loans, at rates averaging around 400% for payday loans and 300% for car title loans, with bank overdraft loans reaching effective rates far higher [S3]. A 36% cap would eliminate those charges. Servicemembers already have this protection; the bill would extend it to everyone [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Sets a maximum 'fee and interest rate' of 36% on any credit extended to a consumer, counting interest, annual fees, cash advance fees, late fees, overdraft fees, over-limit fees, credit insurance premiums, and other add-on charges toward the cap [S3].

Makes loans made above the cap void and unenforceable: the lender must return all principal, interest, and fees, and the borrower could raise the violation as a defense to collection at any time [S3].

Adds criminal penalties — up to one year in prison and a fine of the greater of triple the accrued debt or $50,000 per violation — and lets state attorneys general sue violators in federal court [S3].
Requires credit card statements to display the all-in fee and interest rate as 'FAIR' instead of the conventional APR, so cardholders can see the true cost including fees [S2] [S3].
Leaves state laws that cap rates lower untouched, and strips the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau of authority to exempt lenders from the cap [S3].

analysis.who_pays: High-cost lenders: payday loan companies, car title lenders, online installment and high-fee online lenders, and banks that rely on overdraft fee income. They would lose the revenue streams the bill's findings put at more than $24 billion a year, and some of their current customers — borrowers too risky to serve at 36% — could lose access to any credit at all [S3].

drawbacks.text: A hard 36% cap means some lenders will stop lending rather than reprice, so the riskiest borrowers may be pushed out of legal credit entirely — toward family, unpaid bills, or illegal lenders. The bill's own findings acknowledge this trade-off by calling for 'alternatives to predatory lending' but provide no replacement credit [S3].

Enforcement is unusually harsh for a lending rule: criminal prosecution of individual violators and automatic forfeiture of all principal and interest could sweep in ordinary lenders or debt buyers who unknowingly hold a noncompliant loan, since even 'any subsequent holder of the obligation' must return all payments [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is large and concrete: tens of billions of dollars a year in fees charged at rates of 300% to far higher would end, and the same cap already applies to servicemembers under a 2006 law [S3]. The cost is real but narrower: borrowers at the highest risk would likely lose access to short-term credit, and the bill offers no substitute for it. The criminal penalties and total-void provisions are blunt instruments. On balance, the bill would transfer money from lenders back to struggling borrowers, with the main honest objection being the credit-access gap it would leave behind.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote there, and died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Matt Cartwright introduced the bill on September 13, 2017, joined by 22 Democratic cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day [S1] [S4] [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no markup, no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote [S5].
The bill expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday, car title, and high-fee installment lenders, and banks collecting overdraft fee income, keep their current business models intact because the bill died in committee without a vote.

for.name: Rep. Matt Cartwright
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and authored the 36% national cap, criminal penalties, and state attorney general enforcement provisions.

for.name: 22 of 194 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no Republican cosponsored it.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; the bill sat in committee for the remaining 16 months of the Congress and died there.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat — 23 House Democrats in total — and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on it; no Republican support appears in the record.

industries.note: The bill would cap their products at 36% including all fees, versus rates averaging around 400% for payday loans and 300% for title loans per the bill's findings — eliminating roughly $10.8 billion in annual loan revenue. Its core business model of repeated high-fee borrowing would be illegal.

industries.industry: Banks and prepaid-card providers earning overdraft fees
industries.note: Overdraft fees count toward the cap, and the findings put overdraft fee revenue at about $14 billion a year with effective rates the bill says reach into the thousands of percent. Consumers who overdraw accounts would keep far more of their money.
Triple-digit-rate online installment loans would be capped, and the bill expressly bars regulators from granting exemptions and blocks stronger state caps from being overridden.

Most mainstream cards charge below 36%, but fees — annual, cash advance, late, over-limit — count toward the cap, which would force repricing on fee-heavy subprime cards. All issuers would have to replace APR with the all-in 'FAIR' rate on statements.
